summary: The Alienware AW3423DWF is liked for its deep-black QD-OLED ultrawide picture, strong HDR and fair price, and plenty of owners report no burn-in after years. The biggest complaints are software and firmware quirks, especially washed-out or clipping HDR modes, and quality-control issues such as coil whine and marks. Burn-in and text fringing hit some owners.

The Alienware AW3926QW is praised for sharp text and a vivid, glossy 5K2K OLED picture that works for both coding and games. The main downside is quality control: edge dimming, uneven uniformity with a green tint at the sides, and gaps in the casing, with some units failing early. Experiences vary a lot by unit, and many owners see no problems.

The ASUS ROG Strix OLED XG32UCWMG draws praise for its true-black glossy coating, deep blacks and bright HDR. The dominant complaint is firmware and software: updates that fail or hang, aggressive ABL dimming, flicker and black screens, and input quirks. Quality-control issues such as banding, uneven uniformity and dead pixels also come up.

The MSI MPG 321URX is liked for its stunning picture, strong HDR, handy KVM and good value among 32-inch 4K OLEDs. The biggest complaint is quality control: random shut-offs, lines on screen, wake problems and unwanted pixel-care cycles. Black screens over HDMI and flaky software also come up, and cable swaps or DisplayPort often helped. Many owners report no problems.

Most owners of the Alienware AW3225QF love the picture: deep blacks, strong colour and HDR, and 4K text that many call sharp, with lots reporting no burn-in after long daily use. The main downsides are black-screen flashes and flicker, clunky or buggy software and firmware, and a screen that scratches and smudges easily. Some got eye strain or text fringing.

The ASUS ROG Swift OLED PG32UCDM is liked for gorgeous colour and strong HDR, and many owners report no burn-in after thousands of hours, including heavy office use. Complaints are spread out: software and firmware quirks, random black screens or flicker, and occasional failed units. Some find full-screen HDR dim.

The ASUS ROG Swift OLED PG32UCDM3 is widely praised for vivid colour, good blacks even in lit rooms and strong HDR, with many saying text looks fine. The main complaint is quality control, especially units arriving cracked or damaged from thin packaging, plus the odd display defect. Some notice text fringing or find the stand large and the price high.

The ASUS ROG Strix OLED XG27UCDMG is loved for sharp 4K text on a small screen, vivid QD-OLED colour and good value, especially from discounts and open-box buys. The most common problems are software annoyances, mainly failing firmware updates, frequent pixel cleaning and a touchy proximity sensor, plus a coating that micro-scratches easily. Many report no burn-in.

The ASUS ROG Strix OLED XG27ACDNG wins praise for vivid colour, deep blacks, strong HDR and fast 360Hz motion, and several call its text clear. The main complaints are software and settings quirks such as VRR or G-Sync flicker and black screens, plus connection problems like dropping from 360Hz to 180Hz. A few got faulty units.

The ASUS ROG Strix OLED XG27AQDMG has a glossy WOLED screen with true blacks that happy owners like, and several report no burn-in after thousands of hours. Quality control is the main worry though: grey banding, dead pixels and failures, along with image retention or burn-in for a good number, and text fringing that bothers some.

The ASUS ROG Swift OLED PG27UCDM is praised for very sharp text at 4K on a small screen, rich colour and smooth motion, and many report no burn-in after long use. Downsides are scattered: a coating that scratches easily, a proximity sensor that can blank the screen, and eye strain or headaches for some owners. A few wished it were larger or brighter.

The Gigabyte MO27Q28G has a matte WOLED screen with good blacks and HDR that owners like, especially in bright rooms and for the price. The overwhelming complaint is grey banding and uneven greys, which shows in dark-mode apps and sometimes games and often improves little with pixel cleaning, so many returned it. Others barely notice it in games.

The LG UltraGear 39GX950B is praised for brightness, strong HDR and sharp 5K2K text, and many owners say its light matte coating is better than expected and handles bright rooms well. Others missed the glossy look, finding colours duller or a bit grainy. Quality-control reports include banding, uniformity problems, edge dimming and early failures.

The Dell UltraSharp U4025QW is liked mainly for crisp text and lots of workspace, plus a handy KVM and Thunderbolt hub, especially with Macs. The main snags are connection limits, such as many Macs not reaching 120Hz, and the high price. Gaming motion divides opinion, so it suits work more than serious play.

Most owners of the Alienware AW2725DF praise the vivid, glossy QD-OLED picture and very fast 360Hz motion, and several report no burn-in after years of heavy use. The most common complaints are quality-control problems such as VRR flicker, black screens and early failures, plus text fringing that makes it a weak pick for productivity. A few also got eye strain.

The Alienware AW3425DW is mostly loved for its rich, immersive QD-OLED ultrawide picture and quick response, and several owners say text looks fine. The most common complaint is text fringing that bothers some, especially for work, followed by VRR flicker and a few early burn-in reports. Some found the screen small or got eye strain.

The AOC Q27G3XMN is a budget mini-LED monitor valued for bright HDR, deep blacks for the price and low cost compared with OLED. HDR results are inconsistent though, as a fair number found it washed out, dull or green-tinted and needed lots of tweaking. Other complaints include black smearing, VRR flicker and blooming, plus a few defective units.

The ASUS ROG Strix OLED XG27AQWMG is liked for its bright, glossy tandem WOLED picture, strong blacks and responsive feel. By far the main complaint is grey banding and a dirty-screen effect that varies from unit to unit: some see it only in dark-mode apps, others returned units over it. Many say it is not visible in games.

The LG UltraGear 45GX950A-B wins people over with its size, curve and immersion, plus a bright, good-looking 5K2K picture. Complaints are scattered: DisplayPort and signal problems, flicker or failures, coil whine, and a matte coating or text fringing that some disliked. The aggressive curve and large size put off a few, and it is pricey.

The Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 57" is loved for its huge, sharp workspace that replaces several monitors, and many long-term owners call it the best they have used for work and sim games. The main downsides are reliability and connections: dead units, black screens, DisplayPort 2.1 problems and signal dropouts. Some say it runs hot, and it is very big.
